title: Dynamic equilibrium and Le Chatelier
body: Some reactions run both ways at once. In this tube, brown nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) molecules pair up to make colourless dinitrogen tetroxide (N₂O₄), while other N₂O₄ molecules split back apart.
At equilibrium both reactions run at the same rate, so the colour stays steady. But nothing has stopped: molecules keep pairing up and splitting, in balance. It's a dynamic equilibrium.

Le Chatelier's principle: if you change the conditions, the balance shifts to counteract the change. Pairing up gives out heat, so heating the tube favours splitting apart: more brown NO₂ and a darker colour. Cooling favours pairing up, so the gas turns paler.
realWorld: The Haber process makes ammonia for fertiliser from an equilibrium. Factories choose a temperature and pressure that push the balance towards ammonia while keeping the reaction fast enough to be worth running.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, §13.3 Shifting Equilibria: Le Châtelier’s Principle. https://openstax.org/books/chemistry-2e/pages/13-3-shifting-equilibria-le-chateliers-principle
